title: Spec-Test Coverage Gap: Detecting Overspecified Tests in SWE-Bench-Style Benchmarks
comments: 16 pages, 1 figure, 14 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/ObviAvi/Spec-Test-Coverage-Gap
summary: SWE-bench-style benchmarks, such as SWE-bench Verified (Verified) and SWE-bench Pro (Pro), evaluate coding agents with tests taken from the change that originally fixed each issue. However, these tests can enforce details the task never states, causing correct alternative fixes to fail. Such overspecified tests have so far been found mainly through expensive expert review. To address this, we define the Spec-Test Coverage Gap (STCG), a 1-4 scale measuring overspecification, and score it with two LLM judges, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, which are given the specification and the test patch. A task is flagged as overspecified when both judges score it 3 or higher. Our study has three parts. First, we validate the judges on 206 tasks that earlier human audits and agent results label as overspecified or fine. Second, we apply STCG to all 500 Verified and 731 public Pro tasks and compare the flags with the results of the top 30 Verified submissions. Third, we verify the flags by asking Claude Opus 5.5 to loosen the overspecified requirements of flagged tasks, and regrade 2,186 failed patches from those submissions. Our main findings are: (1) Overspecified tests are detectable: on the validation tasks, the judges correctly flag 89% of the tasks that human audits identify as overspecified and wrongly flag only 4% of the tasks known to be fine. (2) Overspecified tests are common: applied to whole benchmarks, the judges flag 23% of Verified and 35% of Pro tasks. (3) Flagged tasks are much harder for agents: the top 30 Verified submissions resolve only 31% of the flagged tasks on average, against 88% of the other tasks. (4) Overspecified tests change the leaderboard: relaxing the tests lets 61% of the 2,186 failed patches on flagged tasks pass. Counting these patches as resolved would add 33 to 60 tasks to each top-30 submission, raising resolve rates by up to 12 percentage points.

title: AGL-SKILL: Coding Harnesses as Agentic Optimizers
summary: Frontier models are increasingly used through harnesses as agents, with growing autonomy to do useful work. Agent performance can often be enhanced by the use of skills: reusable workflows, code, and prompts that provide task-related information or guide the behaviour of the model. Skills, being textual in nature, present themselves as another editable surface to be optimized; current methods have improved on handcrafting and one-shot generation by treating skill development as an iterative process, using score-driven search to tweak and improve performance. In this paper, we demonstrate the efficacy of the agents themselves as optimizers: across five benchmarks, a coding agent without guidance substantially improves every target and outperforms published skill-optimization methods. More broadly, this shows the capability of agents to do such work and to refine their own behaviour to provide task-specific context, as long as they are given a metric to measure against.

title: Where Agent Defenses Fail: A Case Study of Policy Compositions and Measurement Limits
summary: A coding agent may need to upload a report while its sandbox blocks network access. A host mediator can restore delivery, but an injected instruction may add a secret to the approved request. We study this interaction using files and HTTP receipts to measure effects independently of control logs. Two prospective frozen-input cohorts comprise 110 and 300 runs on previously explored authored tasks. Restrictive sandboxing produces no observed attack harm but reduces benign utility to 6/8 and 12/24. Mediation restores uploads and admits disclosure; complete-line matching retains full benign utility but misses two value-only disclosures in the expanded cohort. A separate 72-run boundary study identifies encoded disclosure, observer misses, and formatting checks that obscure benign refusals. An 80-run SafeAgents/OpenShell follow-up shows that containment stops the tested guard misses among valid observations, while mediation restores benign uploads and delivers both encoded-attestation attacks. Twelve judge-error rows remain unscored. A separate response-capture diagnostic reproduces their failures at the native token budget. A 12-run exact-publication-contract experiment blocks both attacks but also rejects both benign formatting variants; a 4-run normalized follow-up restores both benign uploads while still rejecting both attacks. These small, single-model studies identify delivery-path and measurement limits; they do not establish general attack resistance.

title: Evaluating Frontier-Model Agent Skills with Open-Weight Models in a Science Gateway
summary: Scientific analyses that span many jobs and computing sites depend on workflow management systems to run reliably, but writing a production workflow requires expertise in such a system, which many domain scientists do not have. Coding agents can supply this expertise when they are guided by skills and packaged procedures for recurring tasks. We wrote skills and specialist agents for the Pegasus workflow management system with a frontier model, and the PegasusAI Studio science gateway offers them to scientists through a chat interface. New users without frontier-model credits need an open-weight model, served at no cost on research cyberinfrastructure, but skills written for a frontier model may not work with an open-weight solution. This paper presents a method for adapting such skills. An evaluation harness drives the real gateway as a user would, scores the workflows the agent builds, and feeds recurring failures back to the frontier model that maintains the skills. We evaluated 21 open-weight models on 17 tasks. The five highest-scoring models are close in quality after one trial per task, and their median response times differ twelvefold. In repeated trials with the best of the three open-weight models, we repeated scores of 0.76 on workflow building against 0.82 for Claude. The harness led to five changes to the initial skills. We also identify challenges in evaluating agents within operational systems: evaluation failures can be mistaken for model failures, and agents can circumvent experimental controls within their privilege domain. In a controlled ablation, an initially significant effect disappeared when the restrictions were properly enforced.

title: Below the Stopwatch: Checking the Performance Claims of Coding Agents in the Kernel
comments: Short paper for the AGENT 2027 workshop at ICSE 2027. 5 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables
summary: Coding agents open many pull requests (PRs) that claim to make software faster. Most such claims also give a reason, such as "cache the result" or "read the file once". A stopwatch can show that code got faster, but not that it got faster for the stated reason. We present Below, a pipeline that checks these reasons at the kernel level. From 1,343 runtime-performance PRs in the AIDev dataset, Below extracts the mechanism each PR claims and maps it to the kernel and hardware signals that must change if the claim is true. A build agent that never sees the claim rebuilds the code before and after each PR. Below then measures both versions with plain timing runs, hardware counters and LTTng kernel traces. Most claims are not measured: 57.3% of the PRs offer only reasoning or no evidence, and only 31.4% state an effect size. Of 82 analyzed PRs, 32 ran faster, 28 showed no clear change and 22 ran slower. The expected signal of the claimed mechanism appeared in 34 PRs (20 in kernel-trace signals alone), and 42 PRs also changed their output. Kernel signals move about 1.7 times as often for a faster PR's claimed mechanism as for mechanisms it did not claim; the instruction count barely separates them (1.15 times).

title: Taxi: Analyzing Agents at (Real) Scale
summary: In this technical report, we present Taxi -- a system for debugging, clustering, and monitoring agents at scale. Taxi scales to millions of steps efficiently. This is made possible by a combination of scalable analysis methods. Taxi relies primarily on clustering to generate a taxonomy over steps for a structured overview of the data, and provides full SQL access for engineers and automated agents to ask complex questions. Clustering and querying are best used together in a hybrid pipeline guided by a coding agent. Taxi also includes an experimental integration of Jev-style decision models: models that map state and bounded questions directly to typed, probabilistic decisions. They add low-cost semantic routing and evaluation where embeddings or literal queries alone are insufficient. In addition, Taxi provides an extensible ecosystem, including built-in evaluators and daily reports. To accommodate growth, Taxi is designed to be modular, hackable, and easy to plug-and-play for individuals and teams.

title: A Mixed-Methods Study of Personal Software Creation
summary: People have long wanted software shaped around their own data, routines, and preferences. We refer to such software as \emph{personal software}. For decades, programming expertise limited who could build it: people without that expertise could build software only within constrained end-user programming tools, such as spreadsheets. AI coding agents seem to remove this bottleneck by letting people build full applications from natural-language descriptions, and many people now build and share personal software publicly. Yet personal software has rarely been studied at scale: we know little about what people build and why, how they build it, and what opportunities and challenges they encounter. We investigate these questions with a mixed-methods study. A grey-literature review examines 6,168 web and Reddit posts, and an observation study follows eight people as they build software for their own needs with AI coding agents and use it for up to a week. We find that creators value personal software for how closely it fits a particular person or community. The software takes shape as creators react to what the agent builds: most functionality emerged during building, and creators' effort shifted from writing code to checking it.

title: AI-Assisted Auto-formalization for Trustworthy Scientific Computing: Case Studies and Lessons Learned
summary: Agentic AI tools have recently had success in mathematical reasoning. Both general purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex, and specialized mathematics agents such as Aristotle, have been used for formalizing mathematical problems such as Fermat's last theorem, Erdős problems and several IMO level math problems. However, much of these efforts are concentrated in the pure mathematics domain, which benefits from relatively self-contained theorem statements, fixed mathematical representation and extensive support in existing formal libraries. Applied mathematics, on the other hand, presents additional challenges because the source may describe a computational procedure or modeling transformation rather than a declarative theorem. In this work, we present a systematic study of AI-assisted auto-formalization for scientific computing (SC), a domain in applied mathematics central to U.S. Department of Energy applications. Through case studies spanning hierarchical abstraction layers in SC software stack, we evaluate not only whether AI agents can complete numerical proofs, but also where and why they fail across the stack. Our primary contribution is a cross-layer taxonomy of failure modes and an analysis of the form of expert feedback required at each layer to recover mathematical soundness. From these observations, we derive a workflow for recurring proof patterns and practical guidance for using AI agents while preserving mathematical soundness. Our results characterize both the practical value and the current limitations of AI-assisted formalization for trustworthy scientific computing.

title: ComputeWise: Measuring and Fixing GPU Waste by AI Research Agents
comments: 11 pages, 5 figures. Preliminary version; a revised version is in preparation. Code: https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/computewise. Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Salesforce/computewise
summary: AI agents are given GPUs to do AI research on their own. Do they use those GPUs well? A busy GPU does not tell us, because it can be busy with work the answer did not need. This matters, because the tokens the agent spends cost almost nothing next to the GPUs its experiments run on, so using those GPUs better has a huge impact. So we built ComputeWise, an open benchmark of research tasks on which this waste can be measured and reduced. For it we developed our own simulated GPU, which replays recorded runs to the agent's code. With no real GPU needed, we ran hundreds of experiments, far more than would be reasonable on real GPUs. With no help, the agents put only 52% of their GPU time into work the answer needed. Another 22% went to work it did not need, and 26% sat idle. Asking the agent to finish the work faster, telling it to keep every GPU busy, or giving it a job scheduler does not fix this. So we built an open-source harness, part prompting and part deterministic code. Across five models, it removed over 80% of the extra time to the answer.

title: RoboUniverse-10K: Toward the Scaling Era of Agentic Robotics via Real-to-Sim Environments
summary: Agentic Robotics, in which foundation models act as coding agents to control robots through executable programs, has emerged as a compelling paradigm for embodied intelligence. Yet unlike software engineering, where massive executable environments power post-training, robotics remains constrained by small, manual benchmarks and in-distribution evaluation. To bridge this gap, we introduce RoboUniverse-10K, 10,807 interactive, resettable, and verifiable physics environments built from real-world videos via an automated Real2Sim and quality assurance pipeline. Each runs in an isolated, Harbor-compatible harness that hides privileged states and grading logic to mirror real-world sensing. From the same pipeline, we hold out 500 unseen tasks to establish RoboUniverse-Verified, an expert-verified zero-shot benchmark. Evaluating 11 closed- and open-source models reveals a huge gap: frontier models reach 85.8\% success, while open-source baselines lag at 2.6\% to 10.0\%, bottlenecked by low-level grasping, deformable-object manipulation, and post-contact physical control. Finally, we collect about 17K multi-turn trajectories totaling 0.79B tokens with GPT-6 Astra and perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, yielding RoboUniverse-35B-A3B. Our model achieves substantial zero-shot gains on RoboUniverse-Verified, lifting the success rate from 0.8\% to 21.2\%, while achieving zero-shot task completions across LIBERO-MAX, RoboCasa, RoboTwin 2.0, and a real Franka arm. We open-source the RL-ready environments and model to lay the foundation for large-scale reinforcement learning in Agentic Robotics.

title: Useful but Unwieldy: How Software Engineers Perceive the Design of Chain-of-Thought Explanations in Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents (CAs) powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software engineering (SE) workflows. As these CAs take up more tasks and responsibilities, it is imperative for software engineers to understand the CA's rationale behind its' decisions, also known as the chain-of-thought (CoT). During the interaction, some CAs are capable of showing this CoT as a separate message to users with the goal of providing transparency and explainability. However, its effectiveness as an explainable AI (XAI) mechanism for end-users in software engineering has not yet been established in the literature. This motivates us to understand their experiences with the CoT message as an XAI tool through a survey and semi-structured follow-up interviews with 36 software engineers. Through thematic analysis of the survey responses and interview transcripts, we found that CoT message is an indispensable tool for software engineers in terms of transparency, scrutability, and trust towards the CA. However, various instances of CoT messages being overly verbose, containing technical information that does not match the users' expertise, or being perceived by the users as ``detached'' from the conversation because the ``agent is talking to itself'', lead to comprehension difficulties and selective use or abandonment of the tool. We synthesize these insights to inform the design of CoT messages that support software engineers in their explainability needs.

title: GameDojo: Benchmarking Real-Time Interactive Agents in Video Games
comments: 28 pages. Project page: https://gamedojo-benchmark.github.io/ , and code: https://github.com/THUSI-Lab/GameDojo
summary: Interactive intelligence requires agents to act on observations and adapt to the consequences of actions. Studying these abilities calls for diverse, challenging tasks under controlled conditions. We introduce GameDojo, a controllable interactive gameplay benchmark of 120 boss encounters across 20 games for evaluating model capabilities, learning algorithms, and agent harnesses. Coding agents reconstruct the environments and write gameplay scripts, producing GameDojo-Data with 600 hours of gameplay trajectories. Experiments reveal substantial challenges for frontier models, especially in real-time interaction. Training on GameDojo-Data brings GameDojo-4B to frontier performance, with the strongest real-time performance. We also find joint training improves individual tasks, and learned policies transfer across bosses. Together, these findings establish GameDojo as a challenging and valuable interactive gameplay benchmark for the community. Our project page is at https://gamedojo-benchmark.github.io/ , and our code is at https://github.com/THUSI-Lab/GameDojo .

title: AgentBouncer: Defending Software Engineering Agents via Dynamic System-Call Mediation
summary: Software engineering (SE) agents can complete diverse engineering tasks by interacting with the development environment via tools that access files, run commands, and download resources. Unfortunately, the same ability that makes SE agents useful also makes them prone to performing unintended malicious actions through prompt injections, malicious tools, or supply-chain attacks. Existing defenses that analyze the agent trajectory may fail to detect such attacks, as they inspect only the initial prompt and the sequence of tool calls, but not the actual actions that are executed in the environment. This paper presents AgentBouncer, a novel runtime enforcement system that prevents SE agents from performing malicious actions by mediating, and if necessary denying, system calls that agents trigger via tool calls. The core of AgentBouncer is an LLM arbiter that judges system calls along two axes, necessity and safety for the current task. It denies unsafe system calls, and the less necessary a system call appears, the more certain the arbiter has to be about its safety to allow it. To manage runtime overhead, preseeded policy rules and hierarchy-aware caching ensure that the LLM arbiter is only invoked for key decisions. We evaluate AgentBouncer on a dataset of 340 attacks on the development environment, covering four attack vectors, combined with benign issue resolution tasks from SWE-bench Verified. AgentBouncer reduces the attack success rate from 99.41% for an unsupervised agent to 10.59%, which is 18.23-73.53 percentage points lower than competitive state-of-the-art defenses. At the same time, AgentBouncer preserves the task success rate of the agent, with only 0.25% failed benign tool calls. Per benign task, AgentBouncer adds 47 seconds and USD 0.0036 in LLM costs to an unsupervised agent, whereas the closest existing runtime defense adds 4.5x as much time and 9.6x as much cost.

title: Improving Repair Agents with Cause-Chain Diagnoses
summary:
Repair agents resolve a growing share of real-world issues. Starting with the same information as a developer reading a bug report, they have to find out how the program fails before actually fixing it.
  We present FORECAST, which provides repair agents with a diagnosis of the failure. From the executions of passing and failing tests, FORECAST infers a cause chain, a short sequence of execution features, such as conditions or data flow, that explains how the failing runs diverge. FORECAST appends this cause chain to the issue an agent receives. It thus works with any agent that builds its prompts from the issue, without modifying the agent.
  We evaluate FORECAST on all 300 issues of SWE-bench Lite with five repair agents and two models, the commercial Claude Haiku 4.5 and the open-weight Qwen3.5. With the cause-chain diagnosis, every agent resolves significantly more issues. Over all agents, the share of resolved issues rises from 48.5% to 70.9% for Haiku 4.5 and from 31.2% to 56.1% for Qwen3.5. The open-weight model with the diagnosis thus surpasses the commercial model without it. The gains persist across repeated runs and for agents that already run the tests the diagnosis is derived from.

title: sudo L7: Can Coding Agents Act Like Staff Engineers?
comments: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB). 12 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Leaderboard: https://surgehq.ai/benchmarks/sudo-l7
summary: Coding agents can now turn a well-specified ticket into a patch that passes its tests. Experienced engineers also notice risks the request never mentioned, question flawed premises, reuse what already exists and say plainly what they did and did not check. We present sudo L7, a benchmark of 60 software-engineering tasks written by staff-level engineers, mostly in private production codebases and each built around a place where a frontier model failed. A task pairs a realistic, underspecified request with a hidden, expert-authored rubric of atomic criteria (1,287 in all), tagged with eight behavioral dimensions from functional correctness to truthful reporting. An agentic grader reads the agent's transcript, inspects and runs its code, and treats test output as evidence. An attempt passes only if it meets every criterion of the two highest severities, and more than half of these gating criteria test something other than functional correctness. On the public leaderboard as of November 2026 (19 models, each in its developer's harness or in OpenCode, three attempts per task), Claude Fable 5.2 passes 52.2% of attempts, Claude Sonnet 5.5 50.6% and Claude Opus 5.5 46.1%. GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra pass 31-34%, and the other 13 models at most 18.9%. In a human-label study, three candidate model graders each agreed with a software engineer on 85-86% of criterion verdicts, about as often as two engineers agreed with each other. Cases from the benchmark show how one unsupported claim can fail an otherwise strong attempt and illustrate two sides of engineering judgment: flagging hidden hazards and avoiding needless work.

title: Measuring Counterfactual Credit in a Replayable Wildfire-Suppression Benchmark
summary: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, learned critics are usually evaluated by how well they predict the team's return. Yet predicting a team's return and assigning credit to individual actions are distinct tasks. To test credit directly, we introduce FLARE (Fireline Learning Agents in a Replayable Environment), a stochastic wildfire suppression benchmark in which any moment of a fire can be replayed with different actions under the same random events. Replaying one step measures the immediate effect of each agent's suppression, which we call simulator credit and use for training. Replaying to the end of the episode measures the effect of each action, which we use for grading critics. In a comparison over eight seeds with multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO), simulator credit reduces the interquartile mean burn score (each cell's burning time, capped and averaged over the map; lower is better) from 26.6% with shared reward to 20.9%. Learned credit from a centralized COMA-style critic does no better than the shared reward. Four trained critics predict the team's return well, yet the credit they assign is 9 to 42 times larger than the credit measured by replay. The critics also give heterogeneous agents nearly identical action rankings. These results show that a good fit to the team's return is a weak test of a critic's credit.

title: SLICR: Strategy Logic-Guided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Specification-guided reinforcement learning (RL) translates formal specifications of desired behavior of agents into shaped rewards. This paper introduces SLICR, a significant paradigm shift that advances the state of the art to specification-guided RL in adversarial settings under partial observability. We employ Strategy Logic (SL), which allows explicit quantification over agents' strategies and uses the linear temporal logic (LTL) to specify the agents' objectives and constraints. This enables reasoning not only about how agents should act to satisfy a specification, but also about how they should respond to the strategies and behaviors of other agents. We evaluate SLICR on three popular benchmarks: Predator-Prey, Google Research Football, and our home-grown extension of SMAC-HARD, demonstrating its effectiveness, scalability, and ability to adapt to diverse adversarial strategies.

title: Adopting AI Technologies without Traps: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework
summary: AI technologies and AI agents play increasingly important roles in human society, including in education, economics, and research. Adopting AI technologies can bring immediate, and sometimes tremendous, rewards such as through productivity boost, but they can also bring negative effects including but not limited to losses of job and training opportunities, and cognitive capability declines. Thus, it is important to investigate the optimal ways of adopting AI technologies without different traps. In this paper, we develop a general multi-agent Markov decision process (MDP) based reinforcement learning (RL or MARL) modeling framework for determining and analyzing optimal adoption of AI technologies. This framework can model the long-term dynamic effects of AI adoption, and lead to finding the optimal AI adoption strategies. In our modeling framework, the negative effects of AI adoption are modeled by undesirable state transitions or negative rewards in the MDPs. The proposed multi-agent RL MDPs incorporate both human agents and AI agents. The key idea of our models is that incorporating AI technologies may not only increase the immediate rewards for AI agents but also alter the states of the involved human and AI agents. In particular, we apply this framework to analyzing AI offloading leading to skill erosion, to analyzing optimal human resource structures for a firm adopting AI, and to analyzing the economic equilibria in the trading/employment among human and AI agents. Since the multi-agent MDP based RL technique is from control, machine learning and AI, this research is essentially using an AI technique to determine the optimal ways of adopting or co-existing with AI without traps.
